blocks.title: Script — the mark, standing on its own

segments.text: इ — i — the vowel with no consonant under it.

Since chapter 7 the hand has made ि, the hook that leans in front of the consonant it is read after. A vowel that opens a word has nothing to lean on, so Devanagari gives it a letter that stands on the line by itself.
आ was isolated in chapter 2, ई in chapter 6, ए in chapter 32 for the first number. इ (i) is the fourth, and eleven is what needs it.
Trace इ (i) three times. Write ि beside it and say which of the two can begin a word on its own. Then look at ई and mark the one stroke that separates the two standing letters.
This is the first of the four signs the teens will ask for.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Unicode Devanagari chart.

segments.prompt: Write the standing letter for short i, not its mark.

feedback.correct: That is the letter; ि is the mark that rides on a consonant.
feedback.incorrect: The mark is ि. The letter stands alone: इ.

segments.text: igyārā — eleven.
The count so far stopped at das, ten, and jumped to bīs, twenty. This is the first of the nine words that fill the gap.
Say it in three beats: i-gyā-rā. The middle beat carries a gy cluster that has to stay one sound, not two — the tongue is already at the palate for the y while the g is still closing.

igyārā is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from ekādaśa, "eleven". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 2485); the match is through Hindi igārah and Gujarati agyār. It is eka, "one", and daśa, "ten".
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

feedback.correct: Ten, then the first one above it.
feedback.incorrect: Ten is das. Eleven opens on a vowel: i-gyā-rā.

segments.text: इ (i) + ग्या + रा becomes इग्यारा — igyārā — eleven.

Three pieces, and only the first is new. ग्या is ग with its upright stem cut away and या joined on behind it — the same virama ् you have been writing since chapter 4, doing the job it exists for: two consonants, one breath, no vowel between them.
रा is chapter 1's र with the ा you have written more often than any other mark in this book.

इग्यारा (igyārā) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from ekādaśa, "eleven". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 2485); the match is through Hindi igārah and Gujarati agyār. It is eka, "one", and daśa, "ten".
Copy इग्यारा (igyārā) once while looking. Then write the three pieces apart — इ (i), ग्या, रा — and point at the stem that ग gave up.
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Unicode Devanagari chart.

feedback.correct: Standing vowel, joined pair, then रा.
feedback.incorrect: Build it in three: इ + ग्या + रा.

segments.text: bārā — twelve.

Two is do. Twelve is bārā, and there is no do in it — the b is what is left of an older word for two that Marwari kept only inside the teens. English does the same thing with two and twelve, where the tw- survives and the rest does not.
The ending -ārā is the one igyārā had. From here to nineteen you will hear it again and again: the teens are a set that rhymes.

bārā is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from dvādaśa, "twelve". CDIAL lists Old Marwari bārā under it (CDIAL 6658). It is dva, "two", and daśa, "ten".
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

feedback.correct: Both end -ārā. That is the shape of the whole set.
feedback.incorrect: Eleven is igyārā; twelve keeps only the b of two.

segments.text: बा + रा becomes बारा — bārā — twelve.
Two pieces, no new sign, and both halves take the same ा. ब came in with bīs; र has been in the hand since the first greeting.
Written beside दो, the point the ear made is visible: twelve and two share one letter and nothing else.

बारा (bārā) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from dvādaśa, "twelve". CDIAL lists Old Marwari bārā under it (CDIAL 6658). It is dva, "two", and daśa, "ten".
Look at बारा (bārā), cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write इग्यारा (igyārā) under it and ring the रा that ends both.

segments.text: terā — thirteen.
Three is tīn. Thirteen is terā: the t stays, the long ī flattens to e, and the teens ending arrives. Two beats, both short of effort — te-rā.
You have now heard the pattern three times, and it is the pattern rather than the words that is worth holding: a consonant off the small number, then -ārā or -erā.
terā is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from trayodaśa, "thirteen". CDIAL lists Marwari terā under it (CDIAL 6001). It is "three" and daśa, "ten".
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

feedback.correct: The rhyme is doing the work.
feedback.incorrect: Twelve is bārā; thirteen keeps the t of tīn.

segments.text: caudā — fourteen.
Four is chār. Fourteen keeps the ch and then does something none of the others do: it ends -dā, not -rā.
That is worth marking rather than smoothing over. Three teens in a row have rhymed and the fourth breaks the rhyme, so this is the one in the set most likely to be misremembered as chaurā. It is not.
The au is the diphthong of mausam, the weather word from chapter 16 — the mouth already knows it.

caudā is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from caturdaśa, "fourteen". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 4605); the match is through Hindi caudah and Gujarati cauda. It is catur, "four", and daśa, "ten".
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.prompt: Say thirteen, then fourteen, and say which sound changes at the end.

feedback.correct: The r becomes d. Fourteen is the one that breaks the rhyme.

segments.text: चौ + दा becomes चौदा — caudā — fourteen.
The ौ is the mark मौसम taught, and द has been in the hand since do. Nothing here is new; what is new is the pairing.

चौदा (caudā) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from caturdaśa, "fourteen". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 4605); the match is through Hindi caudah and Gujarati cauda. It is catur, "four", and daśa, "ten".
Write चौदा (caudā) from memory after five seconds. Then write तेरा (terā) beside it and ring the two different last letters — र and द — so the eye records the break the ear heard.
Source: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani.

segments.text: pandarā — fifteen.
Five is pāṅch. Fifteen keeps the p and the nasal, and the -arā rhyme is back after fourteen broke it.
Three beats: pan-da-rā. The nasal in the middle is the same one already in pāṅch — the sound the anusvara writes.

pandarā is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from pañcadaśa, "fifteen". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 7662); the match is through Hindi pandrā. It is pañca, "five", and daśa, "ten".
Sources: Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani; Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages.

segments.text: पं + द + रा becomes पंदरा — pandarā — fifteen.
The dot over प is the anusvara from chapter 3, the one हां needed. There it nasalised a vowel; here it stands for a full n before द. Same mark, and the letter after it decides what it sounds like.

पंदरा (pandarā) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from pañcadaśa, "fifteen". CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 7662); the match is through Hindi pandrā. It is pañca, "five", and daśa, "ten".
